title: Network Share Discovery
summary: Network share discovery is the enumeration step where an intruder lists the folders and drives that other machines expose over the network, in order to find where data lives and which hosts are worth moving into. On Windows networks this rides on the SMB protocol, and the usual tools are the built in net command for querying a remote host share list or the local share list, along with equivalents on other platforms such as the sharing listing command on macOS. The distinguishing artefact is not a malicious file but a burst of directory service and file access traffic: repeated connection attempts to many hosts in a short window, tree connect requests for administrative shares that a user workstation would never open, authentication events for a single account across many machines, and name service queries that map addresses to host names first. Legitimate file access looks similar in form, so the useful signals are breadth, sequence and account scope, because a normal user opens a small number of shares they already know while discovery sweeps many hosts quickly and rarely reads file contents.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker looks around the network for folders and drives that other computers share. A shared folder is one that other machines are allowed to open over the network. Attackers list these shares to find useful files and to spot computers they can reach next.
beginner.whyItMatters: Shared drives often hold documents, backup files and setup scripts. One open share can reveal passwords, plans or customer data. The same list also shows which machines accept connections, which helps an attacker spread. Because listing shares uses normal commands, it is easy to overlook without a baseline of who should be doing it.
howItWorks: The attacker learns which computers are active by scanning addresses on the network.
A command such as net view is run against a remote computer to list its shares.
The net share command is used on a local machine to show its own shared folders.
Shared drives are found through directory queries and connection attempts over SMB, the Windows file sharing protocol.
Each share name hints at its purpose, for example finance, backup or admin tools.
The attacker then opens the most interesting share to read or copy files.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital at night. A visitor walks along the corridors trying every storage room handle to see which ones open. Most are locked, but a few swing open and the visitor notes the room numbers on a map. Nothing is taken yet. The theft happens later, once the map shows exactly which rooms hold the supplies.
takeaways: Discovery is about finding data and reachable hosts, not taking data straight away.
Watch for one account touching many machines and many shares in a short period.
Remove or restrict unused shares, especially administrative ones, and record who opens them.

objectives: Explain what network shares are and why an attacker enumerates them.
Describe the commands and protocols commonly used to list shares on remote and local hosts.
Identify the authentication and file access artefacts this discovery leaves behind.
Explain why volume and breadth separate discovery from normal file browsing.
Describe how share discovery supports later collection and lateral movement.
